segments.say: Lesson 10. Prefix Sum. Precompute running totals to answer any range sum in O of 1, plus "subarray sum equals k" with a hash map.

A prefix sum array stores running totals: P index i equals sum of the first i numbers. Then the sum of any range is one subtraction, P j+1 minus P index i. Here is an analogy. A car's odometer: to know how far you drove between Salem and Bangalore, subtract the reading at Salem from the reading at Bangalore. No need to re-add every kilometre.

Why does this matter? Answers many range-sum queries in O of 1 each. Combined with a hash map it counts subarrays with sum k, even with negative numbers (where sliding window fails). A few key words. Prefix: The first i elements of the array. P index i: Sum of nums 0. i minus 1, with P index 0 equals 0. Range sum: sum(nums i. j ) equals P j+1 minus P index i. Running sum: A total updated as you walk the array.

Core identity. sum(i. j) equals P j+1 minus P index i. Variants: 2D prefix sums for matrix rectangles, prefix X O R, prefix counts (for example number of vowels up to i), prefix products (product of array except self).

Signals. Many range-sum queries on a static array. "Number of subarrays with sum / X O R equals k", "continuous subarray sum divisible by k". Negative numbers present, so sliding window fails.

Problem 1: Range Sum Query: Immutable. Build a class that, given a list once, can answer many queries sumRange(i, j) equals sum of nums index i through nums index j. For example, with nums equals -2, 0, 3, -5, 2, -1; sumRange(0, 2), the answer is 1. -2 plus 0 plus 3 equals 1

The obvious brute force: Loop from i to j for every query. That costs O of n per query. The smart way: Precompute P once. Each query is P j+1 minus P index i. Step by step: In the function Object() { [native code] }, build P with P index 0 equals 0 and P k+1 equals P index k plus nums index k. Then, sumRange(i, j) equals P j+1 minus P index i.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n build, O of 1 per query. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

Problem 2: Subarray Sum Equals K. Count how many contiguous subarrays have a sum exactly equal to k. Numbers may be negative. For example, with nums equals 1, 1, 1, k equals 2, the answer is 2. 1,1 at indexes 0–1 and 1–2
What is it really asking? Because of negative numbers, a sliding window can't decide when to shrink. Prefix sums turn "subarray sum" into "difference of two running totals".

The obvious brute force: Try every start and end index and sum each subarray. That costs O of n squared time. The smart way: For each running sum, count how many earlier prefix sums equal run minus k. Step by step: Keep a running sum and a dict counting how often each running sum has appeared (start with 0: 1 ). Then, At each element, add count run minus k to the answer: each earlier prefix with that value starts a subarray summing to k. Then, Then record the current run in the dict.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n time, O of n space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

segments.sec: Problem 3: Product of Array Except Self
segments.say: Problem 3: Product of Array Except Self. Return an array where answer index i is the product of every number except nums index i. Don't use division, and run in O of n. For example, with nums equals 1, 2, 3, 4, the answer is 24, 12, 8, 6. 24 equals 2 times 3 times 4, 12 equals 1 times 3 times 4,.

segments.sec: Problem 3: Product of Array Except Self
segments.say: The obvious brute force: For each i, multiply all the other numbers. That costs O of n squared time. The smart way: res index i equals (product of everything left of i) times (product of everything right of i). Two passes: prefix products, then suffix products. Step by step: Left pass: res index i equals product of everything to the left of i. Then, Right pass: multiply res index i by the product of everything to the right of i. Then, Both passes are O of n and use the output array itself.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of n time, O of 1 extra (output excluded). Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

A likely interview question: Sliding window versus prefix sum for subarray sums? A strong answer: Sliding window needs non-negative numbers (monotonic). Prefix sum plus hash map handles negatives and counts exact-sum subarrays in O of n.
